props.title: Ben-Hur
props.initialSlug: Epic tale of betrayal and revenge in ancient Rome

sections.content: The 1925 silent epic Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ stands as one of the most ambitious and expensive productions of the silent era, costing nearly $4 million - astronomical for its time. Director Fred Niblo created a technical marvel that influenced epic filmmaking for decades. The famous chariot race sequence, shot with 42 cameras and featuring genuine crashes and injuries, set the standard that even William Wyler's celebrated 1959 remake had to measure up against. The film's massive sets, including a full-scale Roman circus built in Italy, and the groundbreaking use of two-strip Technicolor for select sequences demonstrated how cinema could achieve a scale previously unimaginable.

sections.content: The success of Ben-Hur helped establish the biblical epic as a cornerstone of Hollywood spectacle. Its influence can be traced through The King of Kings (1927) and Noah's Ark (1928), leading eventually to the religious epic boom of the 1950s. The film's remarkable sea battle sequence, featuring full-sized ships and hundreds of extras, demonstrated how cinema could recreate historical events with unprecedented realism. This sequence would influence maritime warfare depictions for generations, from Mutiny on the Bounty (1935) to Master and Commander (2003). SUBHEAD: Technical Innovation and Silent Spectacle

The production's scale required innovations that pushed cinema forward. Multiple cameras running simultaneously, elaborate tracking shots, and the coordination of thousands of extras established new possibilities for epic filmmaking. The film's use of two-strip Technicolor for the Nativity sequence marked one of the earliest effective uses of color in a major production. These techniques would influence later biblical epics like The Sign of the Cross (1932) and Quo Vadis (1951), establishing a visual language for the genre that persists today.
